title: An audience of one
hook: enough are few, enough is one, enough is none

segments.voice: Yesterday: the crowd, and the line was what I bring home. Did you skip one crowd that coarsens you, and what did you bring home instead? Day four hundred forty-two.

A post gets four likes and you feel faintly foolish for having shared it. A song you worked on for months gets a hundred plays. A talk you prepared for gets a half-empty room. Counting the audience is almost automatic now; there's a number under nearly everything we make. Seneca didn't have the number, but he knew the itch. Right after warning Lucilius about the crowd, he ends his seventh letter with three small sayings about how big an audience really needs to be. Today: an audience of one.
screen: `FOUR LIKES.` → `A HALF-EMPTY ROOM.` → `AN AUDIENCE OF ONE.`

segments.voice: First, the setup. Seneca has just said: avoid the crowd. Lucilius might object: then what did I learn all this for, if no one will hear it? Seneca's first answer: you learned it for yourself. So Seneca gives him three sayings, like three small gifts. Second, Democritus. The old philosopher of atoms said, roughly: one person counts as much as a whole people to me, and a whole people as much as one. The size of the audience doesn't change the worth of the work. Third, the craftsman. Someone, Seneca says it's uncertain who, was asked why he took such pains over an art that very few would ever appreciate. His answer: a few are enough for me. One is enough. None is enough. Even no audience at all. The work was worth doing well for its own sake. Fourth, Epicurus. And the third gift, again from Epicurus, the founder of a rival school, writing to a friend who studied with him: I say this not for the many, but for you; we are each a big enough audience for the other. Seneca's point, gathering all three: don't let the pleasure of being praised by many pull you back into the crowd. Do your work well for the one person in front of you, or for no one, and let that be enough. Most of the good in the world is done for an audience of one: a meal for a sick friend, a letter, a careful repair, a child's question answered properly. Nobody counts those. They count anyway.
screen: `WHO WILL SEE MY WORK?` · `DEMOCRITUS: ONE IS A WHOLE PEOPLE.` · `A FEW, ONE, EVEN NONE IS ENOUGH.` · `EPICURUS: AUDIENCE ENOUGH.` · then, large: `ONE IS ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Think of one person who will benefit from something you do today. A coworker who needs your notes. A parent who'd like a call. A kid who needs help with homework. A customer, a patient, a neighbor. Picture their face. Now picture doing that one thing really well, as if they were the whole audience, because they are. No one else needs to see it. Let yourself feel that this is enough. Breathe, and hold their face for a moment longer. The bell holds the time.
An audience of one. Seneca's seventh letter ends with three sayings: one person counts as much as a crowd, and one, or even none, is enough reason to do good work. Today's word.
Your line: one is enough. Do one piece of good work today for one person, and don't count who else notices. Day four hundred forty-two.

screen: `DAY 442 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: ALL MINE IS WITH ME.`

howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism try to do their work well regardless of how many will see it, treating a single person, or no one, as audience enough.

fork.setup: you're a craftsman pouring months into work very few people will ever appreciate. someone asks why you bother. what do you say?
options: a few are enough for me; one is enough; none is enough.
fork.reveal: that's the answer Seneca passes on: the work was worth doing well even with no audience at all.

original.note: Latin: one is enough, from the saying in Seneca's seventh letter.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't worry about likes.
what it means: Seneca says one person, or even no one, is enough reason to do good work; chasing a crowd pulls you back into it.
what a scholar hears: the three sayings come from a materialist philosopher (Democritus), an unnamed craftsman and Epicurus; Seneca borrows freely across schools.

notes: Letter 7.10–11: Democritus 'unus mihi pro populo est, et populus pro uno'; an unnamed person: 'satis sunt mihi pauci, satis est unus, satis est nullus'; Epicurus: 'haec ego non multis, sed tibi; satis enim magnum alter alteri theatrum sumus'. Paraphrased; confirm the order of the three sayings and attributions.
Calling Democritus 'the old philosopher of atoms' and 'a materialist': standard; confirm wording.
'Craftsman' for the unnamed speaker: Seneca says he was asked why he took such pains over an art (ars) that would reach few; 'craftsman' is an interpretive label.

Checked against Gummere (Wikisource), Letter 7.9 to 7.12: order and attributions confirmed (Democritus; an uncertain author, 'content with few, content with one, content with none at all'; Epicurus to a fellow student). Setup now follows 7.9 ('For what purpose did I learn all these things?' and 'it was for yourself'). All paraphrased.
